problem:
Title: Closure of Cartesian Product is Product of Closures

Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be [[Definition:Topological Space|topological spaces]].

Let $T = \struct {T_1 \times T_2, \tau}$ be the [[Definition:Product Space (Topology) of Two Factor Spaces|product space]] of $T_1$ and $T_2$, where $\tau$ is the [[Definition:Product Topology on Two Factor Spaces|product topology]] on $S$.

Let $H \subseteq T_1$ and $K \subseteq T_2$.

Then:
:$\map \cl {H \times K} = \map \cl H \times \map \cl K$
where $\map \cl H$, for example, denotes the [[Definition:Closure (Topology)|closure]] of $H$.

=== [[Closure of Cartesian Product is Product of Closures/Family|Indexed Family]] ===
{{:Closure of Cartesian Product is Product of Closures/Family}}
claim_quote: :$\map \cl H = \Int {\overline H}$
flaw: The asserted equality between the closure of H and the interior of its relative complement is false.
witness: Let X = {0} with the discrete topology, and let H = {0} = X. Its relative complement X \ H is ∅.
explanation: Every closed set equals its closure, so cl(H) = {0}. Also Int(X \ H) = Int(∅) = ∅. Hence cl(H) ≠ Int(X \ H), since 0 belongs to the left side but not the right.

problem: Symmetric polynomials
claim_quote: if n is odd, there is also a term in the form (xy)\^n.
flaw: For every odd n, the binomial expansion of (x+y)^n contains a term of the form (xy)^n.
witness: Work in Z[x,y] and choose the odd integer n=1. Then (x+y)^1=x+y. A term of the required form would be (xy)^1=xy, but the coefficient of xy is 0, so no such term occurs.
explanation: Every monomial in the expansion has total degree n; (xy)^n=x^n y^n has total degree 2n. For the concrete witness n=1, the claimed monomial xy is absent.

problem: Propositional Logic Proof of Substitution Theorem
claim_quote: Let p be a sub-proposition of another proposition P. If you replace p with any other proposition p', then P' is logically equivalent to P.
flaw: Replacing any sub-proposition p of P with an arbitrary proposition p' always yields a proposition P' logically equivalent to P.
witness: Let p=x and P=(x ∨ q), so p is a subformula of P. Replace p by p'=y, obtaining P'=(y ∨ q). Under the valuation x=true, y=false, q=false: P=true ∨ false=true, while P'=false ∨ false=false. Hence P and P' are not logically equivalent.
explanation: Logical equivalence requires equal truth values under every valuation. The displayed valuation gives different truth values, directly refuting the universal claim.

problem: Can anyone check my proof o the second Sylow theorem?
claim_quote: Then for every *h* in *H*, we have hgP = gP, which is equivalent to P = ghg^(-1)P, which is equivalent to ghg^(-1) being an element of P.
flaw: The proof claims that hgP = gP is equivalent to ghg^(-1) belonging to P; in fact, the corresponding condition is g^(-1)hg belonging to P.
witness: Use S3 with right-to-left composition. Let P={e,(12)}, g=(123), and H={e,(23)}. Take h=(23). Then gP={(123),(13)}. Since hg=(23)(123)=(13), hgP={(13),(123)}=gP. But g^(-1)hg=(12)∈P, whereas ghg^(-1)=(13)∉P.
explanation: Thus hgP=gP holds while the quoted condition ghg^(-1)∈P fails. The correct equivalence follows by left-multiplying hgP=gP by g^(-1): (g^(-1)hg)P=P, hence g^(-1)hg∈P.

problem: gcd(a/d, b/d) = 1 iff gcd(a, b) = d
claim_quote: So de is a common multiple of a and b
flaw: From dem = a and den = b, de is a common multiple of a and b.
witness: Over positive integers with juxtaposition as multiplication, take d=2, e=3, m=5, n=7, a=30, b=42. Then dem=2·3·5=30=a and den=2·3·7=42=b, while de=6.
explanation: A common multiple of a and b must satisfy a∣de and b∣de. But 30∤6 and 42∤6. In fact, the hypotheses imply the reverse divisibility: de∣a and de∣b; here 6∣30 and 6∣42.

problem: [Group Theory] Need help understanding proof.
claim_quote: If |A| < |G|, then by the inductive hypothesis both |A| and |G/A| are powers of p
flaw: The condition |A| < |G| suffices to apply strong induction on |G| to G/A.
witness: Let G=Z/2Z={0,1} under addition mod 2, and A={0}. Then A is a normal subgroup and |A|=1<2=|G|. However G/A has the two cosets {0} and {1}, so |G/A|=2=|G|.
explanation: Strong induction at |G|=2 only supplies the inductive hypothesis for cardinalities strictly below 2. Since |G/A|=2, it cannot be applied to G/A. Thus |A|<|G| alone is insufficient; one also needs A nontrivial, equivalently |A|>1 here.

problem: Is this a valid proof for continuity using epsilon-delta definition?
claim_quote: Then for \[; |x-2| < \\delta  ;\] we have \[; |f(x)-f(2)| = |\\sqrt{x}-\\sqrt{2}| < \\epsilon ;\]

problem: [Proof of continuity of x²] Is this an alright proof?
claim_quote: So I have |x²-a²| smaller or equal to |(2a+-1)||(x-a)|
flaw: If |x-a|<1 and the sign in 2a±1 is selected according to the sign of x, then |x²-a²|≤|2a±1||x-a|.
witness: Take a=-2/5 and x=1/10. Then x>0, so select + in 2a±1. Also |x-a|=|1/10+2/5|=1/2<1. The claimed left side is |x²-a²|=|1/100-4/25|=3/20. The claimed bound is |2a+1||x-a|=|-4/5+1|(1/2)=(1/5)(1/2)=1/10. Since 3/20>1/10, the inequality fails.
explanation: Factoring gives |x²-a²|=|x+a||x-a|. Here |x+a|=3/10, whereas the proposed coefficient |2a+1| is only 1/5, so multiplication by the positive value |x-a|=1/2 reverses the claimed comparison.

problem: [University Graph Theory] Proving that a graph is bipartite iff it contains no odd cycles.
claim_quote: Note that since there is a unique path from `[; v ;]` to any other vertex in the graph, this is guaranteed to work.
flaw: In every acyclic graph, after choosing one vertex v, there is a unique path from v to every other vertex, so a single breadth-first search colors the whole graph.
witness: Let G have vertices {1,2,3} and the single undirected edge {1,2}. Choose v=1. G is acyclic: its only nontrivial component is one edge. There is no path from 1 to vertex 3. BFS from 1 visits and colors exactly {1,2}, leaving 3 uncolored.
explanation: The claim confuses an acyclic graph (a forest) with a connected acyclic graph (a tree). In this witness, the asserted unique path from v to every vertex fails because no path from 1 to 3 exists; consequently one BFS does not color the whole graph.

problem: [University Linear Algebra] Is my proof correct? One-to-one composition of linear transformations implies the transformations are one to one.
claim_quote: The claim is that if a linear composition F(G(**x**)) is one to one, where G:U->V and F:V->W, then F and G are one to one as well.
flaw: If the linear composition F∘G is one-to-one, then both F and G are one-to-one.
witness: Over ℚ, let U=ℚ, V=ℚ², W=ℚ. Define G(x)=(x,0) and F(a,b)=a. Both maps are linear. For every x, (F∘G)(x)=F(x,0)=x, so F∘G is the identity and hence one-to-one. However, F(0,0)=0=F(0,1) while (0,0)≠(0,1), so F is not one-to-one. G is one-to-one because G(x)=G(y) implies (x,0)=(y,0), hence x=y.
explanation: Injectivity of F∘G forces G to be injective, but forces F to be injective only on the image of G. Here im(G)=ℚ×{0}; F is injective there but not on all of V.

problem: [High school combinatorics] Where is the fault in my proof by induction?

problem: False proof: Where is the mistake?
flaw: The exponent-reassociation step (-1)^(2/2) = ((-1)^2)^(1/2) is valid.
witness: Over the reals with principal square-root semantics, take base x=-1. Since 2/2=1, (-1)^(2/2)=(-1)^1=-1. But ((-1)^2)^(1/2)=1^(1/2)=√1=1.
explanation: Both sides are defined, but -1≠1, so exponent reassociation fails here. The rule requires additional conditions, such as a nonnegative base.

problem: Is my proof correct?
claim_quote: Functions, where g ◦ f is injective but g is not injective do not exist.
flaw: Functions f,g: N→N such that g ∘ f is injective while g is not injective do not exist.
witness: Let f(n)=2n. Define g(1)=2 and g(n)=n for n≠1. Then g is not injective because g(1)=g(2)=2 with 1≠2. Since 2n≠1 for every n∈N, (g∘f)(n)=g(2n)=2n. Thus (g∘f)(a)=(g∘f)(b) implies 2a=2b, hence a=b.
explanation: These explicit functions satisfy both stated conditions, directly refuting the nonexistence claim. The construction works whether N includes 0 or begins at 1.

problem: how is my proof wrong?
claim_quote: So 1 is the largest natural number
flaw: 1 is the largest natural number.
witness: Take n = 2. Under the standard natural numbers, 2 ∈ ℕ. The claim that 1 is largest requires every n ∈ ℕ to satisfy n ≤ 1, but 2 ≤ 1 is false; indeed 2 = 1 + 1 and 2 > 1.
explanation: A largest natural number must be at least every natural number. The explicit natural number 2 is strictly greater than 1, so 1 is not largest.

problem: Even Prime Month
claim_quote: It turns out, 17 is divisible by lots of numbers (17, 1, etc.) and so isn't a prime.
flaw: The submitted proof claims that 17 is not prime.
witness: Using the standard definition, 17 is prime: 17 > 1, and its only positive divisors are 1 and 17. Any proper factor would have a divisor d with 2 ≤ d ≤ ⌊√17⌋ = 4. Directly, 17 mod 2 = 1, 17 mod 3 = 2, and 17 mod 4 = 1. Thus no proper factor exists.
explanation: Divisibility by 1 and itself is required of every prime, not evidence of compositeness. The exhaustive divisor check proves that 17 is prime, contradicting the claim that it is not prime.

problem: restatement of intuitive theorem for why there are more irrational numbers than rational numbers
claim_quote: for every irrational number, if you divide it by an assortment of different rationals or irrational numbers, you'll always get an irrational number save the sole exception where you ONLY GET ONE POSSIBLE rational number by dividing it by ONE POSSIBLE irrational number.
flaw: For a fixed irrational number, division by irrational numbers can produce only one possible rational result.
witness: Fix x = √2. Choose irrational divisors d₁ = √2 and d₂ = √2/2. Then x/d₁ = 1, while x/d₂ = 2. The divisors are distinct because √2 ≠ 0. Both are irrational: √2 is irrational, and if √2/2 were rational, multiplying it by 2 would make √2 rational.
explanation: The same fixed irrational numerator produces two distinct rational results, 1 and 2, from two distinct irrational divisors. Thus the claimed uniqueness fails.
